newsitem.title: FRANCE: Another poll sees French centre-right lead wider.
newsitem.headline: Another poll sees French centre-right lead wider.

text.p: Another poll has found the centre-right government building on its lead over the left less than two weeks before the first round of France's snap parliamentary election, the Louis Harris polling firm said on Monday.
The latest Harris poll for LCI television found the combined right winning 40 percent of the vote in the first round, an increase of two percent from a similar poll a week earlier.
The combined left would win 37 percent, a dip of one percentage point from the previous week, with the far-right National Front unchanged at 15 percent.
The poll had been scheduled for public release early on Tuesday morning but France 2 television disclosed the findings early.
The Harris survey was the third in three days to show the right widening its lead over the left in the May 27-June 1 National Assembly election.
It did not project how many of the assembly's 577 seats each party would end up holding after the two-round vote.
Curiously, the poll found a growing number of voters predicting a leftist victory despite the right's apparent growing strength.
It found that 57 believed the centre-right would win, a dip of six percent from the week-earlier poll, while 25 percent thought the left would win, an increase of four percentage points for the week.
The rest of those surveyed had no opinion or thought no one would win an absolute majority.

The centre-right's score began mounting in the polls shortly after President Jacques Chirac penned an opinion article for regional newspapers denouncing past Socialist rule and urging voters to give his government a new vote of confidence.
Yet the Harris poll found that just one out of five voters had actually read the article and just 36 percent of those found it to be convincing.
The Harris survey relied on interviews with 871 registered voters conducted on Friday and Saturday.
